newsitem.title: GERMANY: Signs of compromise in German tax reform battle.
newsitem.headline: Signs of compromise in German tax reform battle.

text.p: Signs of a tax reform compromise between German government coalition members and the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) began to appear on Wednesday.

The Cologne-based Express newspaper said SPD parliamentary business manager Peter Struck told it in an interview he could accept a lowering of the top German income tax rate, a part of a major tax reform the government wants to introduce.
Struck was quoted as saying he could accept a cut in the top tax rate from the current 53 percent to 45 percent.

The paper also quoted Rainer Bruederle, deputy chairman of the Free Democrats (FDP), Chancellor Helmut Kohl's junior coalition partners and the most vocal supporters of tax cuts, as saying he was proposing a top tax rate of 41 percent.
Kohl's government has previously said it was seeking to cut the rate to 39 percent and the SPD has insisted that cuts to the top rate were barely able to be financed.

FDP chief Wolfgang Gerhardt, asked to comment on Bruederle's proposal as he arrived in Bonn for coalition talks later on Wednesday on German finances, said only that "it would be good if it came down as much as possible".
The SPD, which controls the upper house of parliament, in April pulled out of talks aimed at getting cross-party support for the reform.
The matter is to be sent to arbitration after which, if no agreement is then found, it will be debated in parliament.
